title: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution: JamPlus
shortTitle: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution: JamPlus
summary: JamPlus is a build utility from the Jam family that reads a .jam file describing what to build and which dependencies it needs, and it supports well known compilers and can generate workspaces for editors such as Visual Studio. This sub-technique covers its abuse as an execution proxy. A .jam file can carry commands alongside the build description, so a reputable signed developer binary performs the adversary's actions as child processes. The behaviour sits alongside the MSBuild case but is rarer, which is precisely why it has been used in campaigns aimed at Windows Smart App Control, where unsigned applications are checked against a cloud list of known good software before they run. Running through JamPlus avoids that check because the launching process is already trusted. Detection rests on a build tool appearing on endpoints that never compile code, on .jam files delivered from temporary or download paths, and on process lineage that places a script or document reader above the build tool.

beginner.definition: JamPlus is a build tool, which is a program that turns source code into finished software. It reads a .jam file that lists what to build and what it depends on. The parent technique covers trusted developer tools in general. This sub-technique is the JamPlus case, where the tool runs commands taken from that file.
beginner.whyItMatters: JamPlus is a normal developer tool and not malware, so it is rarely blocked by security tools. An attacker can hide their commands inside the file that the tool reads. This lets them run code on machines that block unknown programs. Few defenders recognise the tool, so its presence on a workstation is easy to overlook.
howItWorks: The attacker creates a .jam file that contains normal build steps together with their own commands.
The file is placed on the target system, often in a temporary folder or a user folder.
The attacker starts the JamPlus tool and points it at that .jam file.
JamPlus reads the file and runs the commands it contains, usually as child processes.
Because JamPlus is a known developer tool, reputation checks treat the whole activity as trusted.
The attacker's real work happens in the child processes that JamPlus starts, not in the tool itself.
beginner.example: Imagine a plumber arrives at a building with a full toolbox and a work order. Nobody searches the toolbox, because plumbers are expected to carry tools. If the work order says to open a particular cupboard, the plumber simply opens it. The building only checked that the visitor really was a plumber.
takeaways: Any tool that follows instructions from a file can be told to do something else.
A rare build tool on an ordinary workstation is worth investigating.
Look at what the build tool starts, not only at the build tool itself.

objectives: Explain what JamPlus is and what a .jam file describes.
Describe how this sub-technique differs from its parent technique.
Explain how a legitimate build tool can be made to run an attacker's commands.
Identify file and process evidence of JamPlus abuse.
Explain why reputation based checks can still pass in this scenario.
